title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
description: Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a crimin
body: Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.In a victim-impact statement in court, Miriam Haley said the assault had had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions". Weinstein has already spent several years jailed in New York, where he has faced three trials over rape and abuse allegations. He was convicted in a seperate sex-crime case in Los Angeles. This is the second time he has been given a prison sentence in the Miriam Haley case. Weinstein was first convicted and sentenced in 2020, but New York's highest court overturned the conviction in 2024, along with another involving actress Jessica Mann. The court ruled that Weinstein did not get a fair trial.He was retried and convicted again last year on a single charge of a criminal sexual act against Haley.Weinstein, 74, is currently being held in a prison ward at New York's Bellevue Hospital for a series of ailments reported during his incarceration.Once the high-flying producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, Weinstein fell from grace in 2017 after the New York Times and the New Yorker revealed multiple women's allegations of sexual assault stretching back decades. The accusations against him sparked the #MeToo movement, but New York prosecutors have had to navigate a twisting path in securing convictions and sentences.In the 2020 trial, Haley testified that Weinstein had assaulted her in a bedroom in his Manhattan apartment in 2006. Haley was a production assistant on the Project Runway television series at the time. On charges related to Mann, juries could not reach a verdict, and he was found not guilty in another charge involving model Kaja Sokola. After testifying in the retrial last year, Haley told the BBC she felt compelled to take the stand. "I just thought, I have to stand up for myself. I have to stand up for the truth," she said.Weinstein is still awaiting sentencing in the California, where he was convicted in 2022 of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in a hotel room in 2013. An appeals court ordered he be re-sentenced in the case after the New York convictions were overturned.Weinstein has consistently denied the allegations against him, and said he believes he will be proven innocent.On Wednesday, Judge Curtis Farber criticised the former Hollywood mogul as he announced the 15-year sentence."You took what you wanted by force and you have never accepted responsibility," Farber said.

schema.headline: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault

title: Barrecore and Boom Cycle owner suddenly shuts studios
description: The fitness company behind high-end exercise classes Barrecore, Boom Cycle, and Kobox has suddenly shut all its studios.Common Bond emailed customers
body: The fitness company behind high-end exercise classes Barrecore, Boom Cycle, and Kobox has suddenly shut all its studios.Common Bond emailed customers announcing its locations, all of which are currently in London, were closed "until further notice".The firm describes itself as a wellness collective and charges £2,400 for 12 months of unlimited classes. It also runs Reformcore and Triyoga brands and said in August last year it had ten sites.Its website is no longer publicly accessible. The BBC has contacted Common Bond for comment.The email sent to customers on Wednesday seen by the BBC said: "We're sorry to let you know that all Common Bond studios are closed until further notice."We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience and disruption this may cause . We understand this is frustrating, and we appreciate your patience while we work through this."Instructors have told the BBC they were told last week they would not be paid on time and that they only found out about the studios closures from the Wednesday email.One instructor said she and her colleagues were told their pay would be delayed on the day it was due on 14 August.She said: "In good faith, I continued to teach my classes without any news on when or if payment would be made. I have heard absolutely nothing since."

schema.headline: Barrecore and Boom Cycle owner suddenly shuts studios

title: UK warned over ballooning debt costs and slower growth ahead of Budget
description: The UK has been warned over ballooning debt costs and slower economic growth ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next month.The UK was amon
body: The UK has been warned over ballooning debt costs and slower economic growth ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next month.The UK was among countries facing downgraded growth forecasts in a report by the influential Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday.That came as the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) told the BBC that Britain and the US needed to reduce debt due to spiralling borrowing costs.The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war has pushed up the cost of crude oil leading to higher fuel and energy costs, which in turn has driven up inflation around the world.The UK economy will grow by slightly less than expected next year, according to the OECD which now expects growth of 1% next year rather than 1.1%.However, it said the UK had proved more resilient than expected this year, upgrading its forecast for growth 0.9% to 1.1%.Meanwhile, IMF head Kristalina Georgieva told the BBC on Tuesday that global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost"."[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.Inflation has also pushed up the cost of interest on government debt, which alongside an unexpected surge in government borrowing in August has added to the pressure on Healey.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that the UK's high level of borrowing had left it "over-exposed" to global shocks.However, he said he stood by his point - made a year ago -  that Britain should be less "in hock" to investors in the bond markets. At the time, the comments spooked investors due to fears he was calling for spending restraints to be eased. Burnham has made easing the cost-of-living for households one of his key aims, while the government is under pressure to spend more on defence.He and Healey face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households while sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules. The impact of higher fuel prices next year depends on how long supply disruptions last, and stockpiles of oil and supplies from outside the Gulf states have helped cushion the effects on economies so far, the OECD said.Budget airline Ryanair will put up prices next summer as a result of persistently higher oil prices. Chief executive Michael O'Leary said ticket prices will be "materially higher", adding that carriers are in an "almost unprecedented" situation.Ryanair's fuel bill could jump by $1.5bn (£1.1bn) next year to $7.5bn, he said.Risks to the global economy include weaker-than-expected returns on AI investment and climate-change related supply shocks, the OECD said.Next year, global growth is expected to also be 0.1% lower, with countries affected including Australia, Canada, and the Euro-area.Weather-related shocks, including from a strong El Nino, could hit farmers and help push up food prices, it added.In addition, tariffs and export restrictions on trade continue to add to uncertainty, it said. New US tariffs from July as part of the Trump administration's ongoing volatile trade policy have raised its effective tariff rate by 1%.Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said: "Despite unprecedented pressures and conflict in both the Middle East and in Europe, the UK economy is showing strong resilience."She added that the government is "already giving families space to breathe" and "starting the big, long-term changes needed to create good jobs and growth in every postcode".However, Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the OECD urges countries to "control spending and improve public sector efficiency"."Instead, this government is trying to find new ways to tax you whilst having to pay interest rates on their borrowing which are the highest in the G7," he said.Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said that the UK had "so far remained resilient to higher energy prices", but most of that reflected businesses having built up stock and households not putting so much disposable income into savings.However, this effect would be temporary, with growth more muted next year.She added that the "drag" on the economy from energy prices would pick up, while as a percentage of the UK's economic output, debt interest payments are forecast to hit levels seen in the mid-1980s.

schema.headline: UK warned over ballooning debt costs and slower growth ahead of Budget

title: UK military jamming other nations' satellites to defend itself, BBC told
description: The British military has been jamming or blocking satellites from other countries in order to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been tol
body: The British military has been jamming or blocking satellites from other countries in order to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been told.The RAF has been using a ground-based system for the past year, which a defence source said had already been used "to deter our adversaries".It is understood the system could be used to prevent a hostile nation's satellites from tracking the movement of the UK's nuclear armed submarines or other sensitive military operations, such as those involving special forces.It comes as the head of the RAF said the UK faced "unprecedented threats" from adversaries in space, coinciding with the creation of a new RAF unit set up to defend Britain's satellites. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said the new Space Effects Squadron will be focused on "disrupting, degrading and denying hostile threats in space".The squadron will protect British satellites used to warn of incoming missile attacks, provide communications and help guide ships, the MoD said.In a speech on Wednesday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said daily lives depend on satellites that power everyday technologies like mobile phones and banking apps, adding the loss of GPS would cost the UK economy £1.4bn a day."Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries." he said."We depend on them for everything from weather forecasts, energy supplies, and financial transactions to sat-navs, mobile phone connections, and Amazon deliveries," said Streeting, adding that the loss of "everyday conveniences would undermine our daily freedoms, and trust in our institutions."Speaking at the UK Space Conference, Streeting said that threat from Britain's adversaries was growing in "scale, speed and sophistication", adding that the "challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth".A number of nations are believed to have similar ground-based systems against satellites. Last year the then head of the UK's Space Command said Russia was trying to jam UK satellites with ground based systems "every week". The defence source described the UK's terrestrial electronic warfare capability as "world leading, and more".Last week US confirmed for the first time that it had also deployed an unspecified "weapon" in space to defend its own satellites. Both China and Russia condemned the move - warning of an arms race in space. However, Washington has already accused both Russian and China of developing their own space weapons - ranging from electronic jammers, lasers to blind other satellites and even projectiles that can be fired from satellites in orbit.In May, the RAF tracked a series of "dangerous manoeuvres" by five Russian satellites moving close to two Finnish commercial satellites. The RAF's Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth said in June that a Russian satellite constellation had caused disruptions to GPS signals across Europe and Canada.The UK has a handful of military satellites in orbit for surveillance and military communications. But it works closely with the US Space Force - which has many more.In a separate speech at the space conference, ACM Smyth added that "unfortunately we are seeing more and more irresponsible and provocative actions from our adversaries".ACM Smyth warned that without satellites, some of the technologies people take for granted would be lost and would make every sector "less efficient, less prosperous and less secure"."Sat-nav systems would fail, congestion on our roads would be severe and our emergency services would take longer to help those in need," he said, adding that satellites are also needed to monitor the weather and the effects of climate change.

schema.headline: UK military jamming other nations' satellites to defend itself, BBC told

title: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC
description: The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being l
body: The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it"."What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast."So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it."Streeting said the focus now would be to secure a long-term certainty for the base on Diego Garcia, the Chagos archipelago's largest island.He said it had been the view of every UK prime minister since Boris Johnson that an ongoing legal process - as Mauritius argues it was illegally forced to give away the islands in 1965 to gain independence - risks the security of the base.During Trump's first face-to-face meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the UN General Assembly in New York, the US president criticised the "terrible deal" and said the UK was "going to be looking" at it.Burnham replied: "Yep."He later told broadcasters he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution".Burnham added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well."What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it."The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York, and an official readout from that meeting said Burnham "reiterated his commitment to continue doing everything possible" along with the US to ratify the deal.The "review" is not expected to constitute a formal process operating to a specific timeframe.Government sources are insisting that Burnham and Streeting's comments do not represent a major shift from the previous position, which was that any deal would require American support.However Streeting's comments were notable for their explicit acknowledgement that without changes the deal is not going to attract Trump's support.Prior to the pause in April, the UK and Mauritius had signed an agreement in May 2025 and a final draft of the bill to hand over sovereignty of the islands had not passed Parliament.Under the terms of the deal agreed in 2025, Britain would hand sovereignty over the archipelago to Mauritius but lease back the Diego Garcia base for 99 years, which the UK government said would be a net overall cost of £3.4bn.However, Sir Keir, who was then prime minister, came under heavy criticism from opponents who said the real cost of the deal could amount to £35bn, adjusting for inflation, and risked allowing China to establish a presence on the archipelago.Trump, who originally backed the deal, has been a frequent critic of the move, previously branding it a "a blight on our great ally" and an "act of total weakness".Reacting to the review, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to "just scrap this terrible deal".Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God."In 2019, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) gave an advisory opinion that Britain's separation of the Chagos Islands from Mauritius was unlawful and stated the UK must end its administration as rapidly as possible.While non-binding, the ICJ advisory opinion - which was endorsed by the United Nations General Assembly - emboldened Mauritian assertions of sovereignty and led to the UK opening negotiations in 2022.Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday that no money would be handed over to Mauritius "at this stage" while officials review the deal.Describing the Diego Garcia base as "one of the most sensitive and valuable national security assets", he said work was underway to find a deal "that maybe not everyone loves, but everyone can live with".

schema.headline: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC

title: Krystian Bielik: Cardiff City defender charged by FA over Portsmouth incident
description: The Football Association has charged Cardiff City defender Krystian Bielik with misconduct over an altercation involving Portsmouth fans, but a police
body: The Football Association has charged Cardiff City defender Krystian Bielik with misconduct over an altercation involving Portsmouth fans, but a police investigation has been concluded and they will take no further action over the incident.The flashpoint came during Cardiff's 2-0 Championship defeat at Portsmouth on Saturday, 5 September.The FA stated: "It's alleged that the player [Bielik] acted in an improper manner around the 71st minute of the match."The Poland international has been given until Friday, 25 September to respond to the FA charge.Hampshire Police were notified of the incident during the match and launched an investigation immediately afterwards, but this has been concluded.A police statement read: "Following an incident involving a Portsmouth FC supporter and a Cardiff player at Fratton Park on 5 September 2026, we have now concluded our investigation."After speaking with the complainant and reviewing all available evidence, the matter has been resolved by way of an out-of-court disposal, agreed by all parties involved. As part of this resolution, an apology has been provided by the player."The matter is now considered closed, and no further action will be taken in relation to this incident."Cardiff City have been asked to comment.

schema.headline: Krystian Bielik: Cardiff City defender charged by FA over Portsmouth incident

title: Emma Raducanu inspired by Andre Agassi in plotting route back to top of tennis
description: As Emma Raducanu plots a route back to the pinnacle of tennis, the Briton has been taking inspiration from Andre Agassi's 2009 autobiography.Five year
body: As Emma Raducanu plots a route back to the pinnacle of tennis, the Briton has been taking inspiration from Andre Agassi's 2009 autobiography.Five years have passed since Raducanu's remarkable US Open triumph, when at the age of 18 she became the first qualifier in the Open era to win a Grand Slam.American Agassi was a teenage prodigy himself and later claimed the first of his eight major singles titles at Wimbledon in 1992 aged 22.But between the peak years of his career, he had to overcome a challenging period when he went four years without a major and dropped to 141st in the world rankings."I was especially intrigued by the passage where he got out of his slump in the late 1990s by creating his own training regimen and finding his way back to the top," Raducanu told Uniqlo."It speaks in depth about his early successes and the lows he reached, perhaps as a result of them."A lot of it was so relatable."Agassi said his hope was for his experiences to help other players going through similar periods in their own careers."It's wonderful to hear that anybody can relate," Agassi told BBC Breakfast."It was literally the hope that if one person read it and it gave them hope, some tools to understand that they're not alone, they can figure it out and get to a healthier place without having to direct their frustrations at the game of tennis, then it was a success for me."So, hearing that 17 years later it can still impact somebody, especially in this game, it does make me feel good."Raducanu reached a career-high ranking of 10 in July 2022, but the 23-year-old has slipped to 98th in the world.Her progress continues to be hampered by physical issues, and she most recently missed the US Open as she continues her recovery from a stress fracture in her lower right leg.A foot injury disrupted her pre-season training before she spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness earlier this year.But Raducanu enjoyed one of the best weeks of her career at Queen's Club in June, reaching her biggest final since her triumph in New York five years ago.Agassi won all four of the sport's Grand Slams and claimed Olympic singles gold at the 1996 Games.Asked what advice he would give Raducanu, Agassi said: "I would encourage her to focus on being the best of herself on a daily basis, but don't judge that by results or thinking that somehow you have to be 100%."You have to learn to be 100% of whatever percent you're at [and] be comfortable in your own identity inside of that - not what people say."Back in my day, I could just put down the paper and not read it. Now it seems like it's harder for these youngsters to avoid."For Agassi, tennis was by no means a childhood passion. His father, keen for his son to become the very best, would introduce him to others as a future number one tennis player.That additional pressure, Agassi says, led him to play with "fear". It was not until he sank from world number one to 141st that he felt able to reconnect with the sport.Agassi, who created a foundation providing education for under-served children during that time, said: "I had more success from that point forward than I did playing out of fear."The first thing I would advise a parent to think about is that it's not their life, it's their child."You raise a child in their way and they'll never depart from it. You just have to find out what their way is."Agassi will captain Team USA in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London later this week, between 25-27 September."Tennis is a hamster wheel of sorts - the fact that these guys make room in their schedule to play this incredible event tells you how great this event is," Agassi added."We're obviously playing Team Europe, in Europe, so I don't know where the crowd is going to have their heart."But I know one thing - they're going to see some spectacular tennis."

schema.headline: Emma Raducanu inspired by Andre Agassi in plotting route back to top of tennis

title: Man Utd still £1bn in debt, with interest costs rising and £63.5m spent on new stadium
description: In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125m (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on
body: In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125m (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on land for their new stadium. The club has not explained what it has done with the remainder. The stadium itself is likely to cost in excess of £2bn.It means the club's overall debt, while reducing from £1.3bn at the end of December, is still over £1bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £577.6m, the £111.4m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and outstanding transfer fees, which club sources say represents approximated 75% of the £473m listed and being owed as 'trade and other payables'.This comes at a time when supporters are furious about what they believe to be chronic under investment in Michael Carrick's first team squad this summer.United spent £148m on three new signings - Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans - this summer. It was less than a third of the £458m Manchester City invested in their squad and lower even than newly promoted Ipswich.However, fans are angry there was no additional left-back purchased to provide competition for Luke Shaw, who has missed three matches due to injury already, or striking support for Benjamin Sesko, who missed pre-season as he recovered from a shin complaint that has already resurfaced.While United argue the additional funds were earmarked for their stadium, to be built 350 yards away from where Old Trafford stands, the loan itself is lodged within club accounts."We are pleased to have secured record revenues," said chief executive Omar Berrada."This demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, and shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years."While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men's and women's teams during the summer window and our men's team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford."United have also been criticised for a lack of investment in the Women's Super League squad, which is currently second bottom of the table with one point from three games.Ratcliffe previously argued the club had to take strong action to slash losses. Two lots of redundancies led to 450 people losing their jobs, while United have confirmed their latest set of salary costs have reduced by £11.3m to £302m."This is primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men's first team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction programs implemented over the previous two fiscal years," said the club.

schema.headline: Man Utd still £1bn in debt, with interest costs rising and £63.5m spent on new stadium

title: Family 'heartbroken' after mother and three children died in fire
description: The family of a mother and three children who died in a house fire have said they are experiencing an "unimaginable" loss. Elisha Brabin, 36, and her
body: The family of a mother and three children who died in a house fire have said they are experiencing an "unimaginable" loss. Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, 8, and Prudence, 7, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of Tuesday.Paying tribute, their relatives said they had been left "heartbroken" and the loss would be "felt forever". The statement added that "Elisha was a devoted and loving mother" and "our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure".The family said they were "devastated by the loss of Elisha, Leo, Ellis and Prudence"."Elisha was our beloved daughter, wife, mother, sister, auntie, niece and cousin," they said. "She was a devoted and loving mother who lived for her children. They were her whole world, and she meant everything to us."

schema.headline: Family 'heartbroken' after mother and three children died in fire

title: Orkney island welcomes first baby in more than three decades
description: Image caption, Alice Traill Ford welcomed baby Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford in North Ronaldsay last weekByDavid DeldayBBC ScotlandReport
body: Image caption, Alice Traill Ford welcomed baby Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford in North Ronaldsay last weekByDavid DeldayBBC ScotlandReporting fromNorth Ronaldsay, Orkney and Claire Thomson BBC Scotland NewsUpdated 6 hours agoA baby has been born on Orkney's most northerly island for the first time in more than three decades.Parents Jorge Suarez and Alice Traill Ford welcomed baby Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford in North Ronaldsay last week.Islanders toasted the birth with a dram of whisky to celebrate the first newborn in the remote location since Thomas Brookman in August 1992.The family, who split their time between Costa Rica and Orkney and travelled more than 5,000 miles for the birth, said Duncan was born in a much-loved place.Figure caption, I wanted baby Duncan born into the energy of North Ronaldsay"North Ronaldsay has always been a very special place for me and I felt alive and free here every summer when I came up as a little girl," Alice told BBC Scotland News."My intuition was telling me this was the right place for us so we spoke to the NHS to see if it would be possible. "We have this beautiful family home steeped in our history and ancestry so to be surrounded by that felt a very special introduction for him to come to Earth."North Ronaldsay is Orkney's northernmost island and is only accessible from Kirkwall on the main island via a 20-minute plane journey or a ferry, which takes two hours and 40 minutes.The island is famous for its seaweed-eating sheep, which are mostly confined to the shore by a 13-mile-long drystone wall that encircles the island.Image caption, Alice's family still spend holidays at Holland House, which was built by her ancestorsBaby Duncan was born in Holland House, which was built by Alice's ancestors - the Traill family - who bought the island in 1727.The house has been passed down through generations and is still owned by her family.Alice's grandfather, Duncan, was the former Laird of North Ronaldsay and provided the inspiration for her son's name. "I didn't know I was going to name him after Duncan when we arrived but I was sitting on the sofa and right in front of me was a collage of his pictures with my grandmother, so he has been very present with us," Alice said. "He was an incredible man, very kind and really strong and I felt like there would be no better name than his to carry on and continue his legacy in the world."Image caption, The family will return to Costa Rica in NovemberHistorically when the Laird was on the island, a flag was flown at Holland House to inform the residents.So when baby Duncan was born at 04:05 on 15 September, Alice and Jorge followed the tradition to share the news."Over the years we have found a lot of magical four-leaf clovers here and have kept them in a book," Alice said."We stuck a four-leaf clover to a glass bottle, glued a Groatie Buckie to the lid then filled it with whisky and gave it to each of the islanders."We raised the flag and everybody opened their whisky and shared a dram - a celebratory drink - together."A Groatie Buckie is a small, pale pink and white shell found on beaches across Orkney, which in local tradition brings good luck and fortune to the keeper. Image caption, Alice and Jorge gave bottles of whisky with a four-leaf clover and Groatie Buckie glued to them to the islandersImage caption, A flag was raised to tell the islanders baby Duncan had been bornThe family will return to Costa Rica in November, where the couple run a school.But Alice is certain her children will have the same opportunity to spend time in North Ronaldsay as she did growing up."Duncan will absolutely be back every year," she said."One of the things I want to give my children is the gift my mother gave us, bringing us to this island every summer, letting us run wild, explore the island and feel the connection to the community."

schema.headline: Orkney island welcomes first baby in more than three decades

title: Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation?
description: And, at the height of the Coronavirus pandemic, the BBC discovered a network of more than 1,200 faked or hijacked accounts on Facebook, Twitter and Yo
body: And, at the height of the Coronavirus pandemic, the BBC discovered a network of more than 1,200 faked or hijacked accounts on Facebook, Twitter and YouTube that posted pro-Chinese government and anti-US messages.There is evidence to suggest Western governments also engage in disinformation campaigns, although the scale of their operations are not always clear.An investigation by Reuters in 2024, external revealed that during the Covid pandemic, the US military ran a covert anti-vaccine influence operation to discredit China's Sinovac jab.And Meta has previously removed an influence campaign originating from France that targeted a number of countries in Africa, external.AI has also exacerbated the spread of disinformation, as images can now be more easily faked and videos misleadingly edited using text prompts. Text generation has also improved and can create plausible, authoritative and coherent sounding fake news reports.BBC Verify saw evidence of this during US-Israel war with Iran. While in the early weeks of the Russia-Ukraine conflict most of the disinformation published online consisted of old or misleading videos and inaccurate claims, we have seen a deluge of AI-generated images and videos since the Iran war began back in February of this year.Carl Miller, an author and founder of the Centre for the Analysis of Social Media at Demos, told BBC Verify that state-run influence operations "amplify and exploit existing grievances and fissures - making it really hard to work out exactly what sort of effect they might have"."Influence operations are quite fragile things, usually, and we need to find ways of making them much more likely to fail if they target us," he added.

schema.headline: Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation?

title: Nigella Lawson is 'brilliant addition' to The Great British Bake Off, TV critics say
description: Nigella Lawson is 'icing on the cake', TV critics say as she enters Bake Off tentImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Nigella has taken over from Prue
body: Nigella Lawson is 'icing on the cake', TV critics say as she enters Bake Off tentImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Nigella has taken over from Prue Leith as a judge on Bake Off, alongside Paul HollywoodBySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporter TV critics have described Nigella Lawson as the "icing on the cake" of The Great British Bake Off, after the show returned for a new series on Tuesday.Lawson has replaced Dame Prue Leith, who announced she was leaving earlier this year after nearly a decade in the programme's famous tent.The Telegraph said Lawson gives the Channel 4 series a "new lease of life", while Digital Spy agreed she was a "brilliant addition" to the line-up.But the Independent was cooler on the launch episode as a whole, saying the show "wastes Nigella's prodigious charms and misses a chance for a true revamp".The return of Bake Off saw Lawson join fellow judge Paul Hollywood, who has appeared on the programme since its launch in 2010, and presenters Alison Hammond and Noel Fielding. Former Bake Off winner Giuseppe Dell'Anno told BBC Radio 4's Today that Lawson "did produce a step change" to the show and was a "nice fit with the ethos of the programme"."She was doing her best by capturing the vibes of a cake, the feelings, what it makes you think of, which was very nicely balanced by Paul being very technical and scrutinising," he said."I think, however, that she will get better over time, because my gut feeling yesterday was that she was still in new territory."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Some critics noted Lawson did not deliver as much innuendo as expected during her first episodeIn a five-star review, the Guardian's Lucy Mangan said, external Lawson "moves through Bake Off dispensing words of wisdom, generous praise and gentle criticism".She added that Lawson is "just as confident as Leith but a much quieter, more soothing presence that works perfectly with Alison Hammond's ebullience and Paul Hollywood's teacher-ish vibe".The Telegraph's Anita Singh also awarded, external five stars, remarking that "Bake Off and Nigella are a match made in heaven"."She brings glamour, intelligence and poise. And, of course, a hefty dollop of innuendo," Singh said."Lawson is supportive in her judging but not afraid to tell the bakers where they can improve. She gives helpful advice."The launch episode was described as "one of the most disastrous openers ever" by Metro's Adam Miller, external - but luckily he was only referring to the cakes."When Bake Off should be crumbling after 17 seasons, Nigella Lawson is making Channel 4's crown jewel fresher than ever," he said."It's clear to see she is the lifeline Bake Off needed to ensure it could easily have another decade or more in it yet."'Stale format'However, other critics said Channel 4 had missed an opportunity to revitalise the programme.Awarding two stars, the Independent's Nick Hilton said, external Lawson quickly "feels part of the fabric"."But this is also the problem," he continued. "The Bake Off format is very tired. The cakes wobble, the decorations melt, the bakers over-salt the batter, and everything remains the same."Nigella's arrival might have been an opportunity for a harder refresh. But instead of bending the format to suit Nigella, the new judge bends to the will of the programme."Image caption, Prue Leith announced she was leaving Bake Off earlier this yearHilton acknowledged that producers "might have done brilliantly to snag Nigella, and it will undoubtedly lead to an uptick in viewers". "But they've applied her prodigious charms too thinly, and even she – with her preference for all things 'sumptuous' – can't stop the feeling that the show has gone more than a little stale."Several critics noted that Lawson did not deliver as much innuendo as expected during her debut in the tent."Add Nigella – famous for her on-screen coquettish eyelash-fluttering and cheeky language choices – into the mix, and you'd imagine the sauciness gets dialled up to 11,"  said the Radio Times's Jane Rackham, external."Instead, she's cut back on the sauce. She makes well-informed and helpful comments about the amateur bakers' efforts."Digital Spy's Janet A Leigh agreed, external, noting: "As is the nature of Bake Off, there were many opportunities for Nigella to engage with the playful, flirtatious nature that has underpinned the show since its inception. Yet every opportunity was gently rebuffed."Instead, she said, Lawson "has a way of talking about food that celebrates it and expands the audience's understanding of flavours without seeming pretentious"."If episode one is just a flavour of what to expect from Nigella, then it is hugely encouraging. She cares deeply, steers wisely, and slots effortlessly into the close-knit team." Image source, PA MediaWhen Lawson was faced with innuendo-laden comments from contestants or co-stars, she often "wisely said nothing", noted the Daily Mail's Jan Moir., external"Ultimately this was a tremendous debut performance from the new mistress of meringue, showing a side of Nigella we have not seen before: quirky, commanding, funny – but also humane," she concluded.Ben Dowell of the Times observed, external: "Bake Off has always been one of TV's more beguiling offerings with a comforting romance about it. "It's not perfect. Hammond is ebullience and warmth personified but her co-presenter, the erstwhile Mighty Boosh comedian Fielding, still looks a bit lost, as if he has wandered in from the wrong set."But with Nigella the show is definitely in safe hands. Bake Off has found a new star."

schema.headline: Nigella Lawson is 'brilliant addition' to The Great British Bake Off, TV critics say

title: Cristiano Ronaldo: 1,000-goal target and Portugal ambition fuel football icon
description: Cristiano Ronaldo considered retiring after the World Cup but says he opted to extend his glittering career as he believes he can help Portugal to fur
body: Cristiano Ronaldo considered retiring after the World Cup but says he opted to extend his glittering career as he believes he can help Portugal to further success - and reach a personal milestone of 1,000 career goals.The 41-year-old confirmed in the summer that the 2026 World Cup would be his last, although his long-term future remained uncertain.However, he has been included in Jorge Jesus' 25-man squad for Portugal's Nations League campaign, which begins against Wales in Lisbon on Thursday night.In the lead-up to the contest with Craig Bellamy's side, the Al-Nassr forward also targeted the 21 goals needed to reach that magical 1,000 mark.Asked if he thought about retiring from international duty after the World Cup, Ronaldo responded: "Yes, I did."Of course, I'm always thinking on my decisions, my future, the present also. I'm a thinker, you have to think."The former Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus player said: "I had a conversation with our president, with our coach. I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want."I think I can give to the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football."Ronaldo is a two-time Nations League winner with Portugal, and he said adding a third title was also an aim alongside his personal ambitions."Both aims are important," he said."One thousand goals, yes, and the national team. Winning the Nations League, the competition starts tomorrow [Thursday], it's a new age."Young talents including Fabio Silva, Renato Veiga, Nuno Mendes, Joao Neves and Francisco Conceicao all feature in Portugal's squad for this international window.Ronaldo - who joked he will play on for another decade - says helping his country's newest talents was also a pivotal factor in his decision to continue to represent Portugal."This is a new young generation. But for me the basic point is to be on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games," he said."For me, the most important thing, I know what I am. I know what I do to be here, to have the success that I have."I know why young kids love Cristiano, because they see me as an example, and I will continue to do that. Even when I am retired... in 10 years!"I'm happy with myself. It doesn't matter if I play tomorrow, if I rest the next game. For me, the most important thing is that I feel good."

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo: 1,000-goal target and Portugal ambition fuel football icon

title: The heart transplant footballer who won a World Cup for England
description: The footballer who had a heart transplant - then became a World Cup winnerImage source, City Sport Marketing GmbHImage caption, England beat Spain 5-1
body: The footballer who had a heart transplant - then became a World Cup winnerImage source, City Sport Marketing GmbHImage caption, England beat Spain 5-1 in the final of the Transplant World Cup in FrankfurtByJoe LynskeyBBC Sport JournalistWhen Martyn Jackson walked off the pitch after Ramsbottom United's 2-1 win over Cheadle Town in October 2024, it never crossed his mind that one day he could be a World Cup winner.In fact, in the days after that match, his goal was just staying alive.Just a couple of days after the final whistle, Jackson started to feel unwell during the night.He went into hospital and was diagnosed with myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart usually caused by an infection. Within weeks, he was placed on the super urgent waiting list for a transplant.His life was saved when a donor heart became available, and on 28 November 2024, he had successful surgery at Wythenshawe Hospital in Greater Manchester.Fast forward to September 2026, and Jackson scored for England in their 5-1 win over Spain in the final of the Transplant Football World Cup.His team-mates and opponents were, like him, all recipients of a donor organ.Figure caption, England's win at the Transplant World Cup came three days before the start of Organ Donation Week"Obviously, when you've had a transplant, you don't think you're ever going to play again. That's what I thought anyway," Jackson tells BBC Sport."I'll be forever grateful to my donor and the family for what they've given me. They've given me the gift of life and the opportunity to live my life to the fullest."Football at the Transplant World Cup is not quite the same as the game played at the Fifa World Cup.Instead, it reflects how delicate each player's body is having been through life-altering surgery.Matches are seven-a-side and played over 20-minute halves. Contact is "not as aggressive as I was used to", Jackson says.Having played 11-a-side football in the ninth tier of English football before his surgery, he became a game-changing new addition to the national transplant team when he joined up with the squad in January 2026.Jackson spent his youth career in the academy at Manchester United, before spells at Blackburn Rovers, Preston North End and Burnley. He eventually stopped pursuing a career as a professional and spent 13 years with clubs across the non-league pyramid.During his recovery, wife Lucy heard about the opportunity to join an England Transplant FC team on social media.Image source, City Sport Marketing GmbHImage caption, Martyn Jackson won the Transplant World Cup less than two years after receiving a new heartDaley Cross, manager of the England team, said of Lucy's role: "She was just trying to do her best for him and trying to find a way to motivate him."His wife did drop in the conversation that he used to play at Manchester United as a schoolboy. So that got our ears twitched instantly."You could tell from him being on the pitch, even though he was so fresh into his journey, that he knew the football game and he would be such an incredible asset to us."You can be in a dark place, at the time of diagnosis, through your treatment or even post-transplant. So to have us exist to help and inspire people means that we are getting some incredible footballers."And that really is the power of it: to that transplant community or to the world, showing people that when you've had organ failure, your life isn't over. There is a chance for you, and you can go and resume and live your life."As the recipient of a donor heart, Jackson has to manage his exercise workload more carefully than his team-mates, many of whom have had kidney transplants, the most common transplant in the UK.His role in the side tends to involve 10-minute bursts, rather than playing for the duration of matches.Image source, City Sport Marketing GmbHImage caption, Daley Cross manages the England Transplant team alongside his job as a youth workerBayern Munich's Alphonso Davies was diagnosed with a mild form of myocarditis in 2022. He was sidelined for nearly five months, undergoing specialist cardiac monitoring, before returning to play.Jackson started to feel ill two days after Ramsbottom side's win over Cheadle, and his case became so severe that doctors had to fit his heart with a mechanical pump to keep him alive."Of course it was extremely scary," he says, "but at that stage, when you are critically ill, there's not really much you can do about it. You have to accept it."The super urgent waiting list he was placed on is the highest priority of the three tiers of patients waiting for a new heart. Typically, only about four or five people are on the list at any one time in the UK.Dr Paul Callan, a consultant cardiologist at Wythenshawe Hospital's Heart and Lung Centre, worked with Jackson during his diagnosis and recovery."Initially, we used to quote an average wait of seven days on the urgent transplant list," he says. "Now it's up to 14 days. Maybe 10% of patients who are put on the list get too poorly and have to be taken off the list."Image source, Martyn JacksonImage caption, Martyn Jackson was playing for Ramsbottom United in the North West Counties Premier Division in October 2024That increased waiting time is the result of a reduction in the numbers of organ donors in the UK, with a 9% drop recorded in 2026 compared to the same period last year. There are 8,700 people currently waiting for a donor organ, a figure that NHS Blood and Transplant say is an all-time high.This Organ Donation Week,, external which runs from 21-28 September, the NHS has launched an urgent response plan to address the decline.Jackson has yet to meet the family of the donor from which he received his new heart. He says he is considering reaching out to them around the two-year anniversary of his surgery.For him to make a recovery within that time frame, culminating in playing football in a Transplant World Cup, is "remarkable", according to Dr Callan.England beat six teams on their way to winning last Friday's final in Frankfurt, scoring 36 goals, but for every player at the tournament there is gratitude that they even have the opportunity to play a football match again."It is so important to spread that message, have that conversation about organ donation," says England manager Cross, "because our team only exists for that reason."I wouldn't have 16 players to manage if we didn't have organ donation. And England wouldn't have just gone and won a World Cup."

schema.headline: The heart transplant footballer who won a World Cup for England

title: Kimi Antonelli interview: Mercedes driver on moment he knew he had been transformed as an F1 driver
description: Kimi Antonelli says he knew from the first moment he drove this year's Mercedes that he would be transformed as a Formula 1 driver in 2026.The 20-year
body: Kimi Antonelli says he knew from the first moment he drove this year's Mercedes that he would be transformed as a Formula 1 driver in 2026.The 20-year-old Italian, who is running away with the world championship in only his second season in F1, is reflecting on his breakthrough year in the sport in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport.A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards."It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature."Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says."This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change."Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see.After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell.Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune.Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1.The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year.He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would start the new regulatory era with an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite.Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible."I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit."The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy."Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year."If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that."Monza 2024 memory made Antonelli 'afraid to do a mistake'Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend.At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day before they formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza.He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second.Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man."Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down."This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean."Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.'"So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind."Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve."The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together."The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season."Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment."Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment."'First win, first pole, took a lot of weight off my shoulder'Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made."I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great."Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, with the first win, the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder."Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamlessly and quickly. Overtaking moves are done quickly and decisively. There's not been a circuit on which he has lacked pace.Russell, by contrast, has admitted to struggling and - while not trying to take anything away from Antonelli, who he is always quick to praise - has expressed his opinion that his his driving style does not suit this year's new cars.All of which raises a key question - how much of what is happening this year is Antonelli stepping it up, and how much Russell falling back?"That's a very difficult question," Antonelli says. "I've definitely stepped up."This year definitely everything is new. So it requires also a little bit of a different approach. And trying to adapt to a different car, which hasn't been easy."His consistency this year, he says, has come from the fact he has found "a nice rhythm in the season"."I always try to follow my routines," Antonelli says, "the way I approach the weekend. I try to approach it all the time the same."I'm still finding my way, but I've found a way that helps me to be consistent and also helps me to be consistently ready when I go in the car."There are still moments when he misjudges things, though. He cites the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, just days after his outstanding win in Monaco, one of the most dominant at that storied track for years."Monaco was a very high moment for me in the season, and then I went to Barcelona and I was probably a bit too excited, especially over a single lap," he says."So I was overdriving, I was chasing the lap time and the result didn't come in qualifying. I was actually a bit far back and didn't do a good lap."But that's because I was trying to do a bit too much after a very high moment in my career. And then I understood that that is not the way."The lesson was applied after his spellbinding win from 19th on the grid at Monza, his home race, a result that Wolff said "closed a cycle" from his 2024 crash.Antonelli says: "After Monza, I reminded myself, 'Don't make the same mistake as you did after Monaco.'"He won the Spanish Grand Prix seven days later, an eighth victory from 14 races so far this season.Success has inevitably led to fame, and with it attention."Life has changed a lot," Antonelli says. "I'm not going to lie. It's been a big change, but it's nice to see so much support. Definitely, one side is very nice, but on the other side, you have to be careful. You've got to protect yourself a bit more because obviously you're more exposed."All year, Antonelli has talked about focusing on process, about doing the best he can on every single day, not thinking about the big picture.Now, though, for the first time, he acknowledges the title - an achievement that would make him the youngest world champion in F1 history - is on his mind."Yes, I thought about it," he says. "But again, thinking about it, I came always to the same conclusion that the earlier I finish all this, the better it is."So I've got to just keep pushing. I keep doing the best I can every race. Because, yeah, that's the way. Just not finish. And until it's done, it's not over."

schema.headline: Kimi Antonelli interview: Mercedes driver on moment he knew he had been transformed as an F1 driver
